extracted.intended_audience: mathematics-education researchers and college mathematics instructors (particularly IBL and undergraduate linear algebra instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Characterizing and assessing student mathematical modeling and quantitative reasoning in undergraduate courses (linear algebra, differential equations) and identifying critical instructional decisions for inquiry-based learning (IBL) classrooms. Includes design/analysis of tasks, inscriptions, assessment practices, and instructor choices that affect learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical topic areas students draw upon
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which mathematical (and non-mathematical) topic areas students use to reason about a real-world situation (examples observed: calculus ideas about sequences and rates of change; computer programming/algebraic expression construction; psychology/business reasoning; linear algebra/matrix models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare groups' final solutions to see which topic areas they relied on; note that different groups may draw on different domains (e.g., Group 1 used calculus intuition about convergence, Group 2 used programmatic/symbolic computation, Group 4 used matrix models). Use this dimension to characterize variety in student approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and role of inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the inscriptions students develop (external notations, symbolic expressions, diagrams, matrices) and how these inscriptions structure and support their thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inscriptions for how they (1) support computational needs, (2) represent interrelatedness of quantities, and (3) aid conceptualization of the system as a whole. Use student work examples to illustrate how symbolic expressions served computation and further symbolization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning with and about quantities: treating measurable attributes as quantities and building mathematical systems that describe and help reason about phenomena (quoted: 'Quantitative reasoning... can be regarded as modeling').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate students' capacity to identify relevant quantities, measure or estimate them, interrelate them, and use them to construct mathematical descriptions or predictions. Focus analysis on quantitative reasoning related to each group's final solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model quality as conceptual/external systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A model should be a conceptual system expressed using external notation systems and used to construct, describe, or explain behaviors of other systems (Lesh & Doerr, 2003).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this characterization to judge student-created models: are they expressed with external notation, do they explain or predict system behavior, and are they manipulable for intelligent prediction or control?

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of convergence/long-term behavior reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' ability to reason about long-term distribution and convergence (e.g., observing decreasing changes and inferring convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit or implicit arguments about week-to-week change, decreasing rates, and whether long-term distributions depend on initial conditions; note that such reasoning may appear informally even if not used in final formal solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computational simulation vs analytic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish students who rely on computational simulation (e.g., programmatic iteration) from those who develop analytic or symbolic models (e.g., matrices, algebraic expressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether simulation-focused approaches attend to conceptual quantities (differences between weeks) or remain computationally oriented without conceptual generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational efficiency and symbolic design
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs and inscriptions should address computational efficiency and provide symbolism that (1) supports computation, (2) represents interrelatedness, and (3) aids conceptualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge student work for chosen representations that reduce computation, clarify relationships among quantities, and help see the system as a whole (e.g., matrix multiplication to streamline repetitive computations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting tone and expectations (IBL instructor decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors must set the tone and expectations for students in IBL classes as a critical instructional decision affecting success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate course design and first-day/ongoing communications for clarity of expectations about discovery, collaboration, and instructor roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing interpersonal dynamics (IBL instructor decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about how to manage group interactions, classroom norms, and interpersonal issues are central to IBL classroom effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider practices for facilitating equitable participation, conflict resolution, and norms that support student-led inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing student accountability and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors must balance practices that increase accountability (e.g., graded homework) with maintaining a positive collaborative classroom atmosphere; these choices are interdependent and may conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze assessment and participation policies for trade-offs: high accountability mechanisms may reduce collaboration, while low accountability may produce over-dependence and reduced participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-making must be dynamic and in-the-moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Because pacing and activities are often student-driven in IBL, instructors need to make responsive, in-the-moment decisions rather than simply follow prepared notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate instructors' attentiveness, ability to read classroom atmosphere, and flexibility in adjusting activities and supports during class sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some decisions require new solutions aligned with IBL goals
rubrics_metrics.description: As learning goals shift toward constructing and communicating arguments, traditional assessment solutions (e.g., timed individual tests) may no longer measure desired outcomes or fit student experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether alternative assessments (portfolios, presentations, group tasks, standards-based rubrics) are designed to measure the targeted skills and whether instructors have implemented novel solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness of instructional decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: IBL makes many instructional choices explicit that might be implicit in traditional teaching; instructors should surface and reflect on these choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for documented policies and rationales for grading, participation, group roles, and classroom management that make decisions transparent to students and colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practices that instructors commonly report (grading & classroom procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific classroom practices repeatedly mentioned by instructors: grading homework, assigning participation points, selecting students to present at the board, office hours usage, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these practices as evaluative levers: how they are implemented affects accountability, participation, and classroom atmosphere. Evaluate fairness, clarity, and alignment with IBL goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local styles and community constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Local departmental or campus 'styles' of IBL teaching shape instructors' choices and may both support and constrain available practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an instructor's choices, consider local norms and whether practices are inherited, adapted, or deliberately innovated; peer communities can be sources of advice or constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor perspective differences (TA vs faculty)
rubrics_metrics.description: TAs often identify subtleties of classroom decision-making differently than faculty (TAs emphasize implementation quality and student-near perspectives; faculty may attribute issues to student characteristics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multiple instructor perspectives in evaluation and professional development; consider TAs' closeness to student experience when diagnosing classroom issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion-referenced assessment (differential equations course)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should be based on pre-determined and clearly articulated criteria and associated standards of knowledge, skills, competencies and/or capabilities (university policy quoted: 'criterion-referenced approach to assessment').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rubrics/standards that specify expected competencies beyond binary right/wrong; communicate standards to students and align assignments/exams to those criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go beyond right-wrong while maintaining mathematical integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement elements of criterion-referenced assessment in quantitative courses in ways that go beyond simple 'right-wrong' criteria but still maintain the mathematical integrity of the assessment program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples or rubrics that describe competency levels, partial-credit rationales tied to conceptual/technical competence, and ensure rigorous mathematical correctness where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional point-allocation grading versus standards-based criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional grading often assigns points at stages of a written 'correct' solution; criterion-referenced approaches instead map solutions to standards/competencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating assessments, compare whether marks reflect attainment of stated standards (competency-based) rather than accumulation of points for reaching intermediate solution steps; consider transparency and student perceptions.
